item.title: PM greets Hindu community on Durga Puja
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Friday extended greetings to the Hindu community in Bangladesh and across the world on the occasion of Sharadiya Durga Puja, one of the major religious festivals of the Hindu community.
In a message on Friday, he said that, according to Hindu beliefs, Goddess Durga comes to earth from heaven for the welfare of the world, ensuring the well-being of her devotees, destroying evil forces and nurturing creation.
“The destruction of evil forces and the worship of truth and beauty have given a unique significance to Sharadiya Durga Puja,” he said.
The prime minister said people of different faiths, groups and communities in the country would observe their respective religious festivals with great enthusiasm.
He said the celebration of religious festivals reflected the beauty of Bangladesh's age-old religious and social values and cultural traditions.
He said friendship, harmony, goodwill and fraternity among people of different religions, groups and communities as Bangladeshis were manifested through religious, cultural and social activities.
Tarique Rahman said: “Equality, human dignity and social justice are fundamental to all religions, while the welfare of humanity is one of their principal teachings.”
“Therefore, alongside practising their respective religious beliefs and cultures, it is essential for everyone to maintain an atmosphere of peace in society through mutual respect, honour and compassion among people,” he said.
Referring to the country's political transition, the prime minister said Bangladesh had once again embarked on the path to democracy following the ouster of fascist rule at the cost of thousands of lives.
He said a massive undertaking to rebuild the country had begun, adding that the government's commitment was to establish a welfare-oriented, safe and humane Bangladesh for all citizens, irrespective of political opinions, religion or ethnicity.
“May our diverse society and outlook on life be enriched by the message of harmony and amity. Religion belongs to individuals, while the state belongs to all. Everyone has the right to security, regardless of religion,” he said.
Addressing members of the Hindu community, the prime minister urged them to celebrate the festival across the country with enthusiasm, joy and confidence, without fear and in safety.
He extended his greetings to the Hindu community once again on the occasion of Sharadiya Durga Puja.

item.title: Food Directorate: Affordable food, climate resilience top priorities
item.description:
Ensuring affordable food for low-income households, maintaining adequate public grain reserves and strengthening emergency food distribution amid climate-related disasters are among the government’s key priorities, according to the Directorate General of Food.
The government plans to strengthen subsidised food distribution, improve beneficiary selection and expand digital monitoring of food prices and supplies to enhance food security, particularly for vulnerable communities.
Md Jamal Uddin, additional director general of the Directorate General of Food, said: “Ensuring affordable food for low-income people, maintaining adequate public stocks and delivering emergency food assistance quickly during climate-related disasters remain our key priorities.”
Despite progress in food production, access to safe and nutritious food remains a challenge for many households in Bangladesh. Rising living costs, limited purchasing power and growing climate risks continue to put pressure on food security.
Under the Food-Friendly Programme for the 2026-27 fiscal year, 5.5 million beneficiaries are set to receive 30kg of rice per month for six months at Tk15 per kg.
The programme aims to ease food expenses for low-income households and ensure access to essential staples during periods of financial hardship.
Meanwhile, the Open Market Sale (OMS) programme is operating in 419 upazilas, selling rice at Tk30 per kg. Subsidised rice and flour are also being distributed through more than 1,000 sales centres nationwide.
The effectiveness of these initiatives will depend on timely deliveries, adequate supplies at sales points and ensuring that eligible households can purchase commodities at the announced prices.
The government also plans to strengthen public food grain procurement, maintain adequate reserves and improve distribution networks. Better beneficiary selection is another priority to ensure assistance reaches the poorest households and those most vulnerable to food insecurity.
Digital monitoring of food prices and distribution is expected to help authorities identify shortages, delays and implementation gaps more quickly.
Particular attention is needed for households struggling to afford nutritious food, as access to sufficient calories alone does not guarantee a healthy diet.
Effective implementation and transparent monitoring will be essential to ensure that public spending on food assistance delivers tangible benefits.
Bangladesh remains vulnerable to floods, cyclones, droughts, river erosion and salinity intrusion in coastal areas. These hazards can damage crops, disrupt livelihoods and interrupt food supply chains.
Crop losses and transport disruptions can reduce food availability in local markets, while declining household incomes can make essential commodities increasingly unaffordable.
To address these risks, coordination among the ministries responsible for food, agriculture and disaster management and relief, alongside other relevant agencies, will be crucial.
Planned measures include pre-positioning food grains in disaster-prone areas, protecting government warehouses and transport infrastructure, and ensuring rapid food distribution during emergencies.
The government also aims to work with development partners to support climate-resilient agriculture and vulnerable coastal communities, including smallholder farmers.
Strengthening early warning systems, emergency preparedness and local supply networks could help minimise disruptions and ensure affected communities receive assistance when they need it most.
The global food security situation underscores the need to make food affordable and accessible, rather than focusing solely on increasing production.
According to the Food and Agriculture Organization's The State of Food Security and Nutrition in the World 2025 report, an estimated 733 million people worldwide faced hunger in 2024, or approximately one in every 11 people.
The figures highlight the need for coordinated action to improve food access, strengthen nutrition and make food systems more resilient to economic and environmental shocks.
The theme of World Food Day 2026, “Innovation Today, Nutrition Tomorrow,” highlights the role of innovation and improved food systems in addressing hunger and malnutrition.
For Bangladesh, the challenge is to ensure that gains in food production translate into affordable, nutritious meals, particularly for households living in poverty and climate-vulnerable areas.
Progress over the next year will need to be assessed through indicators such as programme coverage, timely distribution, food availability and affordability.
During disasters, the speed of emergency food delivery, the extent of supply disruptions and the preparedness of vulnerable communities will also be important measures.
Ultimately, implementation will be the main test of the government's commitments. Ensuring that 5.5 million beneficiaries receive their allocated rice on time, maintaining adequate supplies at OMS outlets and reaching the intended recipients will be crucial to the programmes' success.
As Bangladesh faces mounting pressure from rising living costs and climate vulnerability, the effectiveness of its food security efforts will depend on reliable delivery, strong oversight and preparedness at the local level.

item.title: Four die after gas cylinder blast in Narayanganj
item.description:
All four people who suffered burn injuries in a gas cylinder blast in Kachpur, Narayanganj, have died, including a husband and wife.
The latest victim, Rony, 19, died while undergoing treatment at the National Institute of Burn and Plastic Surgery in Dhaka on Friday morning.
Dr Sultan Mahmud Shikder of the institute confirmed his death.
Earlier, Rozina, 30, died on the afternoon of October 14. Her husband Sharif, 34, died early on October 15, while her brother Riaz, 22, died later that day.
Rozina suffered burns to 60% of her body, while Sharif and Riaz sustained burns to 40% each. Rony had burns covering 70% of his body.
The blast occurred around 1:30am on October 10 in a room on the second floor of a six-storey building in Sonapur, Kachpur.
Four people were severely burned in the explosion, which was reportedly caused by a gas cylinder leak.
The victims were identified as tenant Rozina, her husband Sharif, her brother Riaz and another tenant, Rony.
Hearing the blast, local residents rushed to the scene and rescued the victims before taking them to the National Institute of Burn and Plastic Surgery in Dhaka for treatment.

item.title: Man loses 3 fingers in sound grenade explosion in Gazipur
item.description:
A 45-year-old furniture trader lost 3 fingers when a sound grenade he picked up beside a rubbish dump exploded in Sreepur, Gazipur, on Friday morning.
The incident occurred around 9am in the Satiabari area of Rajabari Union in the upazila. Members of the Special Response Battalion (SRB) Gazipur Porabari Camp, the SRB Dhaka Bomb Disposal Team and Sreepur police visited the scene.
Debajit Paul, squad commander of the Special Response Battalion-1 (SRB-1) Gazipur Porabari Camp, said information from the bomb disposal team indicated that the device was a police sound grenade lost from a police station on August 5.
The injured man, Nur Mohammad, son of Abdul Khalek, is a furniture trader in the area. Local residents rescued him and took him to Shaheed Tajuddin Ahmad Medical College Hospital in Gazipur, where he is receiving treatment.
Police and local residents said Nur Mohammad had gone to urinate near a pile of rubbish beside his shop. After noticing an object resembling a cocktail bomb in the pile, he picked it up and handled it.
Unable to identify the object, he pulled out its safety ring, causing it to explode and sever 3 fingers on his left hand.
Sreepur Police Station Officer-in-Charge Mohammad Shahinur Alam said Nur Mohammad had picked up a plastic or container-like object from a pile of rubbish behind a shop and carried it to the front after returning from urinating.
Several people sitting there warned him not to handle the object. However, it exploded while he was handling it, severing 3 of his fingers.
Police are investigating how the object came to be there. Legal action will be taken following an investigation into the incident, Shahinur Alam added.

item.title: Mahdi Amin: Govt to support best young talents for international UN conference
item.description:
Prime Minister’s Adviser for Education and Primary and Mass Education Mahdi Amin on Friday said the government will provide all-out support to send the best young talents selected through national-level competitions to the international conference at the United Nations Headquarters in New York.
“After selecting the best young talents through national competitions, the government would send them to the international conference at the United Nations Headquarters to develop their talents, creativity and leadership skills,” he said while inaugurating the "Bangladesh Youth Model United Nations 2026" at the LD Hall of the National Parliament.
Future Bangladesh, youth organization, organized the two-day conference where students from schools, colleges and universities across the country were scheduled to take part in mock debates on national and global policy issues.
Mahdi Amin, also Prime Minister's Office (PMO) spokesperson, said special initiatives were being taken to provide students with opportunities to engage in international platforms.
“A national competition will be organized across the country, with young people from every school, college and university participating. The ultimate winners will be sent, with government funding, to an international conference at the United Nations headquarters in New York so that they can represent the red and green flag of Bangladesh on the global stage,” he said.
The adviser said that the government would extend all necessary cooperation to formally implement the initiative from next year under the prime minister’s directive.
He said the prime minister had adopted a unique triangular approach to developing students’ talent and creativity through education, culture and sports.
Under the initiative, government patronage would continue for talent-development activities and competitions across the country, including mathematics and physics Olympiads, Natut Kuri, Quran recitation and hifz competitions, debates and quizzes, he added.
Recalling his student life, Mahdi Amin said he had participated in Model United Nations in 2007 while studying at Baruch College of the City University of New York and visited the UN Headquarters as a representative of the college.
The adviser said young people had played a leading role in every major turning point in Bangladesh’s history, from the Language Movement of 1952 and the Liberation War of 1971 to the anti-autocracy movement of the 1990s and the July mass uprising of 2024, shedding blood to pave the way for freedom.
The present government was committed to creating opportunities for young people to realize their potential based solely on merit, competence, integrity and justice, without consideration of any particular political identity, he added.
Deputy Speaker of the National Parliament Barrister Kayser Kamal, Chief Coordinator for SDG Affairs at the Prime Minister’s Office Professor Dr SM Abdul-Awal and Dr David Dowland, registrar, Office of the Registrar Controller of Examinations, of BRAC University also spoke at the ceremony.

item.title: Seven arrested over leaked job exam questions, 5 govt employees among them
item.description:
Seven people, including five government employees, have been arrested over the leak of question papers for the recruitment examination for assistant youth development officer posts under the Department of Youth Development, the Special Response Battalion (SRB-3) has said.
The syndicate allegedly charged candidates Tk8–10 lakh each, according to preliminary findings.
The arrestees are Md Rubel Islam, 33, a data entry operator at the Department of Environment; Md Mofizul Islam, 23, a job seeker; Md Hasinur Rahman Sujon, 32; SM Imdadul Islam, 35, a computer operator at the National Board of Revenue (NBR); Asadul Islam, 33, an office assistant at the Ministry of Defence; Nur Mohammad, 30, an office assistant at the NBR; and Jahangir, 38, a computer operator at the NBR.
Lieutenant Colonel Faizul Arefin, commanding officer of SRB-3, disclosed the information at a press conference at the battalion's media centre in Kawran Bazar, Dhaka, on Friday.
He said the team seized a set of question papers, 116 Tk100 stamp papers, four Tk50 stamp papers, 19 pages of admit cards for various examinations, 15 certificates of different categories, 48 pages of bank cheques from various banks, one bank cheque, eight mobile phones, six national identity cards and Tk4,000 in cash.
Investigators have yet to identify the original source of the leaked question paper. Although the arrestees claimed to have obtained it through Facebook, they failed to provide satisfactory evidence to support their claims, the SRB-3 chief said.
The recruitment screening test for 242 assistant youth development officer posts was scheduled for October 10. A total of 319,000 candidates applied for the examination.
The test was due to begin at 11am, but the authorities postponed it after confirming the leak at 10:03am that day.
SRB launched a covert investigation following the incident and arrested the seven suspects in separate drives across Dhaka and nearby areas between October 14 and 16. The Department of Youth Development filed a case with Motijheel police station on October 11.
According to Lieutenant Colonel Faizul, Rubel, Mofizul and Sujon were arrested in Motijheel on October 14. Based on information obtained from them, Imdadul was arrested in Uttarkhan, while Asadul was detained in Mirpur-10 with assistance from SRB-4.
After analysing the suspects' mobile phone conversations and chats, SRB-4 arrested Nur Mohammad in Savar on October 15. Information and evidence obtained from him subsequently led to Jahangir's arrest in Mohammadpur on October 16.
An analysis of the suspects' mobile phone chats showed that Nur Mohammad first received an unclear image of the question paper from an unidentified source at 4:43am on October 10. At 6:15am, Jahangir sent him a clearer image of the paper.
Nur Mohammad then prepared the answers and sent them to Jahangir and Imdadul. The question paper and answers were subsequently distributed among other syndicate members and candidates associated with the group.
Asadul, Rubel, Mofizul and Sujon were also involved in the operation, the SRB-3 chief said. The syndicate allegedly used fake identities on WhatsApp to carry out its activities.
Asked who had initially supplied the question paper to Nur Mohammad, Lieutenant Colonel Faizul said identifying the source was a key part of the investigation. Nur Mohammad, however, failed to provide a satisfactory answer.
Both Nur Mohammad and Jahangir claimed they had obtained the paper through Facebook, but investigators have yet to verify their claims. The Facebook groups and accounts they mentioned are being examined, he said.
“We will try to identify the original source from which the question paper was leaked,” Faizul added. He said the investigation was ongoing to trace the source of the leak and identify others involved.
Asked whether any official or employee of the Department of Youth Development was involved, the SRB-3 commander said investigators had so far found no direct evidence linking anyone from the department to the incident. However, employees of other government offices had been found to be involved, and further details could emerge as the investigation progressed.
He also said Mofizul joined the syndicate in hopes of making more money after being defrauded by one of its members. The investigation had also uncovered financial transactions linked to admission-related business, he added.

item.title: Durga Puja begins in Gopalganj, Sunamganj with festive fervour
item.description:
The five-day Sharadiya Durga Puja, the biggest religious festival of the Hindu community, began in Gopalganj on Friday with Maha Shashthi rituals, including the invocation and ceremonial welcome of the goddess.
According to the traditional calendar, this year's celebrations will continue for six days, ending on Wednesday, with Bijoya Dashami and the immersion of idols.
The festivities began gathering momentum on Thursday evening, when temples and puja mandaps across the district were illuminated with colourful lights and decorated with elaborate pandals, ornate gates and eye-catching designs. The sound of drums and conch shells added to the festive atmosphere as devotees visited the mandaps to offer prayers, take photographs and celebrate.
Priests performed Shashthi rituals on Friday morning, formally welcoming Goddess Durga to the mortal world from her heavenly abode on Mount Kailash, accompanied by her four children — Lakshmi, Saraswati, Kartik and Ganesha.
The goddess's face will be unveiled at the mandaps on Saturday, marking Maha Saptami. Saptami rituals will continue tomorrow, followed by Ashtami on Monday, Navami on Tuesday and Dashami on Wednesday.
This year, Durga Puja is being celebrated at 1,288 mandaps across Gopalganj's five upazilas and four municipalities. Security has been strengthened at the venues to ensure peaceful celebrations.
Sanjay Sikdar, general secretary of the Gopalganj district unit of the Puja Udjapan Parishad, said devotees would bid farewell to the goddess through idol immersion on Dashami, before welcoming her again the following year.
Dipankar Chakraborty, a priest at Shahapara Temple in the town, said the goddess arrived this year riding a horse and would depart by boat. According to traditional beliefs, the two modes of transport symbolise social uncertainty and agricultural prosperity, respectively.
Durga Puja is also being celebrated at 445 mandaps across Sunamganj. The five-day festival began on Friday with Maha Shashthi and will conclude on Bijoya Dashami.
The Special Response Battalion (SRB) has stepped up surveillance on social media to prevent rumours and misinformation that could disrupt communal harmony during Durga Puja.
Its cyber team is monitoring Facebook, Instagram and other platforms around the clock, said Wing Commander Tajminur Rahman Chowdhury, commander of SRB-9 Sylhet.
He made the remarks on Friday after inspecting security arrangements at the Durgabari Puja Mandap in Sunamganj town.
He said bomb disposal teams were ready to respond to reports of suspected explosives near puja mandaps. Drone surveillance, special patrols and dog squads have been deployed, while speedboats remain on standby for remote areas. Helicopter support will be provided if necessary.
A strong security cordon has been established across the four districts under SRB-9 to maintain law and order, he added. The force will remain on duty until Bijoya Dashami, the final day of the festival.

item.title: Besieged Yemen city faces looming healthcare crisis
item.description:
Crammed with beds and stretchers, the dilapidated Al Jumhuri hospital in Yemen’s besieged city of Taiz is running so low on fuel and medicine that it may have to close, officials warn.
With pro-Iran Houthi fighters surrounding Taiz and blocking all supplies, the facility is symptomatic of a collapsing health system in Yemen’s third-largest city, they say.
At Al-Thawra General Hospital, Taiz’s biggest, the kidney center is treating 420 patients. But its generators have just 14 days’ worth of fuel, its director Youssef al-Zakri said.
“We don’t know what will happen to them” after that, he told AFP during a visit this week. Without dialysis, they will die, he warned.
One of the patients, Ahmed al-Issai, needs two treatments a week and never leaves his hospital bed.
“A dialysis patient is like a fish. If it leaves the water, it dies,” he told AFP.
Houthi fighters have encircled Taiz since early October, blocking the road that links it to Aden, interim capital of the Saudi-backed, internationally recognized government.
The Houthis, from Yemen’s rugged north, seized the capital Sanaa in 2014, sparking a brutal civil war with a Saudi-led coalition fighting for the government.
After a years-long lull, the conflict -- which triggered a major humanitarian crisis -- has flared again during the US-Iran war, impacting Yemen’s beleaguered populace once more.
“Most of Taiz’s medical facilities are threatened with closure due to the lack of diesel,” Ilan Abdulhaq, Taiz’s deputy governor in charge of health affairs, told AFP.
She also lamented “a shortage of medicines and medical supplies, which are impossible to find because of the total blockade” on the city’s entrances imposed by the Houthis.
Discussions have taken place to set up humanitarian corridors, but “we have received no assurances in this regard,” she added.
Fadl al-Bukhari, who suffers from a heart condition, says the shortages are increasingly acute.
“The pharmacies say: ‘It’s not in our hands. There is a blockade, the medicines have not arrived,’” he said.
Across Yemen, hospitals and health facilities are “overwhelmed” by the most intense fighting in years, the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) warned this week.
Clashes in Taiz governorate and along the Red Sea coast left hundreds of fighters dead and displaced more than 100,000 people, according to military sources and the UN.
“Frontline hospitals are receiving large numbers of wounded people with limited supplies of surgical materials, anaesthesia, oxygen and medicines,” ICRC health coordinator Feras Abusamra said in a statement.
The World Food Program (WFP) said the renewed fighting has left it unable to reach 600,000 people in Taiz who rely on humanitarian aid, including 200,000 women and children.
Taiz governorate has “some of (Yemen’s) highest levels of food insecurity,” with 10 of its 16 districts classified at emergency levels, the WFP said this week.
“The latest monitoring indicates that wheat flour stocks are nearly depleted while local markets are running out of food,” it said in a statement.
According to the WFP, more than 18 million people -- most of Yemen’s population -- are facing severe food insecurity. About 2.2 million children under five suffer from acute malnutrition.
“We are critically concerned about the escalating conflict, but even more so about the growing number of people we can no longer reach because of it,” said El-Khidir Daloum, WFP country director in Yemen.
“This is the kind of situation that can rapidly spiral into a humanitarian catastrophe,” he added.

item.title: India detains top ‘cockroach’ movement leader
item.description:
Indian police detained Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) leader Abhijeet Dipke on Friday ahead of fresh protests demanding the removal of the country’s election chief, the youth-led movement said in a social media post.
Dipke, 31, was detained shortly before a protest called by the online movement at Central Park in Connaught Place, a busy commercial district in the heart of New Delhi.
“Abhijeet is detained by Delhi Police!!! This government is so scared of the youth waving national flag!!,” the CJP said on social media.
The group as well as opposition parties have been seeking the resignation of India’s chief election commissioner over a large-scale voter roll revision that they say favors Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s ruling party.
The Election Commission of India, which oversees voting in the world’s most populous nation, has denied any wrongdoing.
Dipke had urged supporters to carry national flags and gather at Central Park after two of his colleagues were detained for breaching security barricades at Jantar Mantar, a protest site declared off-limits by police this week.
Thousands of security personnel were deployed in central Delhi on Friday, with police warning protesters to stay away, citing orders restricting public gatherings.
In the past week, the Indian capital has seen several street protests against the electoral roll revision, which was overseen by Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.
More than 133 million names have been removed from electoral lists under the exercise, according to figures reported by Indian media and cited by opposition parties in court filings.
Critics say the removals have disproportionately affected minorities, particularly Muslims.
Election authorities say the move was intended to eliminate duplicate, deceased and fraudulent entries.

item.title: Elon Musk unveils Tesla’s ‘flying’ car
item.description:
Tesla CEO Elon Musk unveiled what he described as a “flying” car, equipped with thrusters, during a livestreamed event at his SpaceX rocket company’s facility on Thursday.
Technical and regulatory challenges have so far prevented the much-hyped flying car sector from getting off the ground.
Musk revealed his new Roadster sports car during a launch event at a SpaceX test facility in Texas.
During the demo, which was livestreamed on Tesla’s X account, the car launched from a steep steel ramp and performed a full barrel roll in mid-air before landing on its wheels.
“Flying cars are real,” Musk said during the event.
Musk said that while the vehicle’s “success is not guaranteed... it will probably work.”
The two-seater sports car did not have a driver for the demo “to make sure we don’t kill anyone,” he added.
Musk said the car was equipped with 10 nozzles and “ultra high-pressure air tanks” to propel itself into the air and accelerate quickly on the ground.
The car can go from 0 to 60 miles per hour (100 kph) in under one second and reach a top speed of 230 mph (370 kph).
The tech billionaire described the development as “what happens when you have a collaboration with the world’s best car company and the world’s best rocket company,” referring to Tesla and SpaceX.
“It can basically fly like a rocket,” he said.
Musk said the Roadster was “not necessarily a safety-optimized car” but it would “be an actual car that’s on the roads.”
“I’m not sure it’s necessarily legal in all jurisdictions, but there will be such a car that someone can own,” he added.
Musk said the vehicle would go into production in 2028, though he’s known for announcing release dates for his Tesla or SpaceX products that end up being pushed back by several years.
The unveiling of the Roadster was postponed many times and had been expected for at least nine years.
On Tesla’s website, interested customers can reserve a “Performance” Roadster model or a “Thrust” model, with boosted thrusters. The final sale price has not been disclosed.
American aviation pioneer Glenn Curtiss debuted the first flying car prototype in 1917.
But successful designs have become more seriously contemplated only in recent years as electric motors and high-performance batteries have advanced.

item.title: Four killed battling Indonesia fires as toxic haze cloaks region
item.description:
Four people died on Indonesia’s Java island fighting the blazes that have sent toxic smoke across southeast Asia, closed schools and fueled a surge of respiratory complaints, authorities said Friday.
The impact of the months-long fires has also prompted Singapore’s leader to vow legal action against any companies responsible for the blazes that have made regional air quality among the world’s worst.
Singapore again topped IQAir’s live ranking of the world’s most polluted major cities on Friday, with Kuala Lumpur second and Jakarta eighth.
“Where warranted, we will take action under Singapore’s Transboundary Haze Pollution Act, and also explore joint action with other countries,” said Singapore Prime Minister Lawrence Wong, without giving further details.
The law allows authorities to target companies whose activities overseas cause or contribute to unhealthy haze levels in Singapore
Legal experts have cautioned that pursuing companies linked to the smoke is challenging, with investigations reliant on cooperation from foreign authorities.
Singapore has no plantations or forests of its own, but several companies with concessions in Indonesia are reportedly based in the city-state.
Singapore’s investigations into four Indonesian companies over their alleged role in the 2015 haze crisis remain open, a case that strained relations with Jakarta at the time.
An official at Indonesia’s national police investigations agency on Wednesday said it was probing companies responsible for the fires, but did not give specific names.
Indonesia experiences wildfires regularly during its dry season, but this year the blazes have been especially severe because a strong El Nino has brought drought.
While drought contributes to the fires, experts say deforestation and drying of peatlands has damaged previously fire-resistant landscapes.
“We cannot control the weather or the winds, nor can we directly control what happens beyond our borders,” said Singapore leader Wong.
“But we will do everything we can to protect Singaporeans, while working with our neighbors to address the underlying causes of the haze.”
On Friday, the city-state’s air pollution surged to around 251 on IQAir’s Air Quality Index level into very unhealthy levels at around 0400 GMT.
Under the Swiss-based company’s system, readings of 151-200 are considered unhealthy, 201-300 very unhealthy and above 300 hazardous.
A local Singaporean tour guide, who asked AFP not to use his name, said “You can’t see much from Singapore’s famous landmarks.”
“Usually I can see as far as the national stadium. Today we can’t see anything,” he added.
The smoke is a direct consequence of the fires, which four people lost their lives battling in East Java’s Bromo Tengger Semeru National Park on Thursday, Indonesia’s forestry ministry said.
Two others suffered serious burns and were receiving further medical treatment.
“This incident serves as a reminder that forest and land fire extinguishing is a high-risk operation,” it said, adding that personnel safety remained a primary concern.
The forestry department in the same statement said there was a significant jump in hotspots in several areas in six “priority provinces” where 615 so-called hotspots were detected.
A hotspot is a location where a satellite detects an unusually high temperature, indicating a potential fire or other strong heat source.
In Indonesia’s Palangkaraya, a city in central Kalimantan, air pollution levels hovered in the hazardous zone above 300 on Friday, according to IQAir.
But many residents did not wear face masks, and stall owners went about their business as usual, but the ongoing haze had an impact.
“It leads to shortness of breath, and in terms of business, there’s an impact,” said Syehan, 43, who goes by a single name like many Indonesians.
“People travelled from afar to go to the market to purchase staple food. Nowadays, they don’t go to the market anymore,” Syehan said.
The haze has also affected regional aviation in Indonesia.
Since the haze first hit on August 11, more than 2,020 flights were affected, civil aviation chief Lukman F. Laisa said.
Of these, 1,067 were cancelled, 919 flights were delayed and 18 other flights were diverted to other airports, Lukman said in a statement shared on Friday.

item.title: Starlink: How Elon Musk’s company influences geopolitics
item.description:
Lack of internet access is a major problem in many regions of the world today.
Starlink was initially developed by the American tech billionaire Elon Musk to solve this problem. It was designed as a way of quickly getting the internet into regions all over the world where this was either impossible to do by conventional methods, or so expensive that it wasn’t worth attempting.
Since then, Starlink’s field of application has widened significantly. It’s used as a means of communication in disaster zones, but also by armies or protest movements, for example in regions where the existing internet has been destroyed by enemy fire or shut down by authoritarian governments.
But there is a downside: Ukraine’s military, for example, is heavily dependent on Musk’s satellite system. This has become especially apparent as the service faces external disruption.
Starlink, which is operated by Musk’s SpaceX company, is a satellite-based system consisting of 10,000 small satellites located around the world. They transfer data packages via laser links and do not require a constant, direct visual link to a ground station.
Unlike other internet satellites, which orbit at around 36,000 kilometers (22,000 miles) above the Earth, Starlink satellites are only about 550 kilometers up. This means they can transmit internet signals much faster than the others.
All users need is a small receiver terminal with an electronically controlled antenna, which automatically steers toward the satellites as they pass overhead. The terminals receive signals from these satellites and transmit them to a nearby router, which supplies the broadband internet connection.
Ukraine: Since the start of the Russia’s full-scale war in February 2022, Starlink has become a vital instrument of communication in the war zone. The Ukrainian armed forces use Starlink to coordinate units, operate drones and control unmanned ground systems. In the civilian sector, the system is used by hospitals, emergency services, energy suppliers and the railway network.
Ukraine offers a particularly vivid example of how heavily its military capabilities now depend on Starlink.
In mid-October, Ukrainian army units reported disruptions to data transmission, which are said to have severely affected the control of combat, interceptor- and reconnaissance drones. Elon Musk said that restrictions on the speed and use of Starlink are determined by the US military and ultimately the US president. At this stage, it remains unclear who ordered the restrictions.
Iran: In early January 2026, protests erupted all across the country against the regime in Tehran. The government’s hardline response included a nationwide internet shutdown. Reportedly, thousands of Starlink terminals were smuggled into Iran and sold on the black market. This enabled the protest movement to go on coordinating demonstrations against the regime, using Starlink to circumvent state censorship of the internet.
The country’s authorities are cracking down on the satellite service and its users. Mohammad Amin Aghamiri, the secretary of the Supreme Council of Cyberspace, described Starlink as a hostile “tool of war” and said the regime had means at its disposal to disrupt satellite connections.
Starlink is officially banned in Iran. Anyone using the service faces a prison sentence of six months to two years. If users are also charged with endangering national security or espionage, the offence can even carry the death penalty.
Sudan: In the Sudanese civil war, Starlink is used primarily by the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), a paramilitary group fighting against the internationally-recognized government. Hundreds of devices were smuggled into the country via the United Arab Emirates, and there is now a thriving black market for Starlink terminals in Sudan. The RSF use them to communicate and coordinate with their militias, while the Sudanese Armed Forces are trying to block both the import and use of the terminals.
Venezuela: Here too, Starlink has been used in the past to sidestep information blackouts and secure access to the internet. For a long time, the service was only available unofficially, by buying kits from local dealers. Following the US intervention in early January 2026, during which then-head of state, Nicolas Maduro, was taken prisoner, Musk offered the people of Venezuela a month’s free broadband internet service via Starlink.
Gaza: Starlink has been used for humanitarian purposes in the devastated Gaza Strip since July 2024. Aid organizations and a field hospital use it to facilitate telemedical assistance and logistical coordination. Access for civilians remains limited because of Israeli security concerns.
Starlink is often the only way to access the internet in conflict zones. This gives Musk and his operating company SpaceX tremendous influence. Previously, for example, Musk refused to activate Starlink in Ukraine to enable an attack in Crimea. US President Donald Trump has also threatened to switch off the satellites in Ukraine, as a way of forcing Kyiv to make concessions in peace negotiations.
There has also been criticism from an ecological perspective. The Starlink satellites have a lifespan of less than five years. Every day, on average, one or two of them burn up in the Earth’s atmosphere. This releases aluminum oxide, which could affect the ozone layer, contributing to global warming. In addition, all those thousands of satellites reflect the sunlight, making the night sky brighter, and this may also have repercussions for the world’s animals.
In an effort to break Starlink’s monopoly, other companies, especially in Europe, are already working on alternatives. At present, the biggest private competitor to SpaceX is a company called Eutelsat. With a fleet of over 600 satellites, its OneWeb service is far smaller, focusing on business customers and maritime use.
But Eutelsat is also involved in the development of IRIS2 — an acronym for Infrastructure for Resilience, Interconnectivity and Security by Satellite, an ambitious EU project to establish a highly secure satellite network. The aim is to make Europe less dependent on Starlink, but IRIS2 won’t be fully operational before 2032.
Elon Musk also has competition inside the US from another billionaire, Jeff Bezos, whose company Amazon is currently working on Amazon Leo, known until recently as Project Kuiper. This is establishing a network of more than 3,200 new low-Earth-orbit satellites. Amazon plans to roll out the service later this year in the US, Canada, France, Britain and Germany.
The sky is clearly getting crowded. China is also refining two satellite communications systems of its own. Guowang, a state project conceived primarily for national and military purposes, will consist of up to 13,000 satellites, while another project, Qianfan, with an estimated 12,000 satellites, is more commercially oriented and aims to provide services to newly industrialized and developing countries. The first mass starts for both of these projects are planned for this year.

item.title: Russian, Bangladeshi short films screened in Dhaka
item.description:
The Dhaka International Mobile Film Festival (DIMFF), with support from the Russian House in Dhaka, organised a special film screening titled “Russia–Bangladesh: Two Nations, One Screen” in Dhanmondi, Dhaka, on October 15, 2026.
The event brought together students, filmmakers, faculty members and invited guests to explore the cultures, perspectives and storytelling traditions of Russia and Bangladesh through cinema.
The programme featured six short films selected for DIMFF, including three Russian and three Bangladeshi productions.
’Russia–Bangladesh: Two Nations, One Screen’ film screening organized by the Dhaka International Mobile Film Festival with support from the Russian House in Dhaka in Dhanmondi on October 15, 2026. Photo: Courtesy
The Russian films were The Shell, directed by Oleg Kondratiev; Raspberry, directed by Mariya Sergeevna Klenovskaya; and One Minute, directed by Ilnur Mukhambetaliev.
The Bangladeshi films were Sound of Silence, directed by Shoumik Bakshi Dipto; Goodbye, directed by Jannatul Ferdos Akhi; and Hurumturum, directed by Sohan Sheikh.
The screening offered audiences an opportunity to experience the creative work of filmmakers from both countries and explore how cinema conveys cultural experiences, human emotions and diverse perspectives.
During the opening session, Alexandra A. Khlevnoy, director of the Russian House in Dhaka, highlighted the importance of cultural cooperation between Russia and Bangladesh.
She encouraged young people to nurture their creativity, explore new ideas and continue learning through cultural and artistic engagement.
’Russia–Bangladesh: Two Nations, One Screen’ film screening organized by the Dhaka International Mobile Film Festival with support from the Russian House in Dhaka in Dhanmondi on October 15, 2026. Photo: Courtesy
Professor Dr Sumon Rahman, dean of the School of Social Sciences and head of the Department of Media Studies and Journalism at the University of Liberal Arts Bangladesh (ULAB), welcomed the participants and emphasised the role of cinema in connecting people, sharing perspectives and deepening mutual understanding between cultures.
Mir Wadud Islam, instructor of DIMFF, spoke about the significance of the screening and the role of filmmaking in storytelling.
The programme concluded with remarks by Sohan Sheikh, festival director of DIMFF, followed by a vote of thanks from Syeda Sadia Mehjabin, adviser of DIMFF 2027.
The screening brought Russian and Bangladeshi short films together on a shared platform, highlighting cinema’s role in cultural exchange, creative expression and people-to-people connections.

item.title: Make polluters pay: From Mannar to the world, communities demand
item.description:
At Keeri Beach in Mannar, in Sri Lanka’s far north, about 250 people stood together under the scorching sun in blue gowns, lining the water’s edge with hands joined and arms raised toward the sea.
Who is responsible for climate change? Who will pay for the loss and damage? People from every walk of life kept asking as they took part in an installation by Indian artist Dr Subodh Kerkar for Greenpeace South Asia in the second week of October, ahead of the 31st Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (COP31).
An art installation by Dr Subodh Kerkar at Keeri Beach in Mannar, Sri Lanka, calls for climate justice and accountability, urging polluters to pay for the damage caused by climate change. Photo: Courtesy
A fish processor in Senegal described her family home shrinking from more than 20 rooms to 6, a fisherman in Mannar reported his catch falling from 300kg to 30kg, a campaigner from Papua New Guinea spoke of islands lost to the sea, a cab drivers’ association leader in Hyderabad highlighted drivers enduring hours of extreme heat without shade, and a Bangladeshi participant described hydration points set up in markets for vendors and rickshaw pullers.
Their homes and workplaces are thousands of kilometers apart, but the complaint was the same: those who did the least to cause the climate crisis are living with its effects every day, and those who caused the loss and damage must pay for it.
For Mama Fatou Samba, a fish processor and community leader from Senegal, the sea’s advance is measured in meters and in relatives.
“Forty years ago, we had to swim more than 100 meters to reach the sea. Now, the sea has advanced by more than 100 meters.”
In her area, the coastline reportedly retreats 2 to 3 meters a year, and the water has reached the ground where her house stands.
The family home once had more than 20 rooms; now, only 6 remain as the sea advances, relatives are forced to leave, and a household that had lived together breaks up.
Mama Fatou Samba called that breakdown one of climate change’s most painful consequences, sometimes worse than the financial loss.
Fishing and farming can no longer support a family, she said, and thousands of young people take risky routes to reach Spain and Italy, many from her area.
“They are climate refugees.”
Vinzealhar Ainjo Nen, a participant from Morobe Province, Papua New Guinea, said a culture tied to land and sea by ancestors is now under strain from rising waters, erratic weather, food insecurity and floods.
A participant from Papua New Guinea wearing her traditional dress attended at Mannar. Photo: Ali Asif Shawon/Dhaka Tribune
“For generations, my people have lived with the land and the nature around us, but that has changed. Severe weather events, forest fires, and water scarcity are adversely affecting my community. It is not our actions that cause this, but the choices of those who do not recognize or care about the hardship we face. I came to Mannar because our voices must be heard, and listened to,” she said.
Mannar gave her something else.
“I’m not alone,” she said, describing how people tied to the land can feel stuck “in a bubble.”
Restituto del Rosario, a fisherman from the Philippines, speaking through a translator, delivered a short, grave message: it may already be too late, and the world could lose its fish and the food that comes with them.
“Because our livelihood depends on fishing, extreme heat is hitting us hard. We did not create this crisis, but we live with its cost. Standing here in Mannar with communities from across the world, our message is simple: the fossil fuel companies responsible for this must pay,” he said.
Qunson Marynathan, an independent climate researcher based in Mannar, said that after nearly 30 years at sea, his catch used to be 300 to 400kg, but now it is 30 to 40kg.
Qunson compared that day’s temperature of about 31 degrees Celsius with a 30-year October average of around 30 degrees, a rise of roughly 0.8 degrees.
These are his own readings, not an official record, but his larger point does not depend on them: Mannar sits among very shallow seas, and shallow water heats easily.
His grievance was with how outsiders study the place.
“What goes missing in the eyes of many reporters or researchers is the people,” he said.
Mannar hosts many migratory bird species and has been inhabited for some 2,000 years, appearing on Ptolemy’s maps.
“When you take us, the people, out of the equation, it’s not there. Come talk to me first,” he said.
He described heat as something the body feels.
“Go to the streets under the sun on a very heavy day. You try to negotiate with somebody who’s selling something, and they start shouting at you. This is not the culture of the people. This is also being caused by climate change.”
His children had been unwell for days.
“I didn’t heat up the sun. I didn’t heat up the ocean,” he said.
Dr S Wijeyamohan of the University of Vavuniya’s Department of Bio-Science said the ocean absorbs heat and carbon dioxide, stabilizing the climate, but that capacity is not unlimited.
A Bangladeshi participant, Kouser Alam, described a response already underway on the streets.
With Greenpeace’s help, they set up hydration points in major markets over the past year, serving vendors, rickshaw pullers and construction workers.
“We are not just raising our voice against these issues. We are trying to solve the issue also,” Kouser said.
An art installation by Dr Subodh Kerkar at Keeri Beach in Mannar, Sri Lanka, calls for climate justice and accountability, urging polluters to pay for the damage caused by climate change. Photo: Courtesy
Shaik Salahuddin, a cab drivers’ association leader from Hyderabad, said drivers and delivery workers move between air-conditioned cars and punishing outdoor heat all day, a strain on body and mind.
He said platform companies advertise concern for gig workers, “but that is only from PR.”
At Hyderabad’s international airport, drivers wait 4 to 5 hours in a car park with 4,000 to 5,000 vehicles, no trees and little shade.
Platforms pay ₹10 extra when it rains, he said, but nothing when the heat turns dangerous.
“The platform companies are also not accountable and transparent,” he said.
Guidelines exist, but “only on paper, not in real realities.”
Meenakshi, a street vegetable seller from India, described a squeeze from both sides. Vendors buy extra water to sprinkle on produce and wet sacks to cover it. Costs rise while earnings fall because fewer customers want to shop in the heat.
Amanullah Porag, a youth climate activist from Bangladesh, said: “Where I live, rising water is not a prediction — it is already taking land, homes and livelihoods. Families are being pushed to move, again and again. This is not a natural disaster; it is the result of decisions made far away from us, by companies that have profited while we lose everything. We came to Mannar to stand in solidarity with global south communities as accountability cannot wait any longer.”
Why in Mannar? When asked, Binu Jacob, executive director of Greenpeace South Asia, said: “Mannar is unique in many ways, with its rich biodiversity, its connection to the ocean and communities that have depended on the sea for centuries. But what is happening here is not just a story about Mannar. It reflects the experiences of fishing and farming communities across South Asia and around the world.”
“Those who contribute least to climate change are often paying a heavy price for the lifestyles and economic activities of others. Climate accountability means asking why these communities must bear the consequences while industries and countries continue to profit from carbon-emitting activities and pollute the environment,” he said.
“We have only one planet. Communities worldwide are already raising these concerns, and we are joining their efforts to share their experiences with a wider audience. Our aim is to help people see the connections between climate change, livelihoods and responsibility,” said Binu, who joined Mannar with a team of volunteers by cycling more than 300 kilometers from Colombo.
Dr Subodh Kerkar, a doctor who became an ocean artist, called the installation “a protest and a prayer.”
Artist Dr Subodh Kerkar talking about his works at Mannar. Photo: Ali Asif Shawon/Dhaka Tribune
“Art is not a slogan. Art is a whisper. Art has to be subtle. We don't have to shout, ‘I love the ocean’ or ‘I want to protect the ocean.’ Standing together in the water and raising our hands is itself an act of protection, an act of connection and an act of love for the ocean,” he said about his artwork at Mannar.
“The life of a fisherman and the life of the ocean cannot be separated. The ocean is very much a part of a fisherman's life, and that inseparability is what I try to express through my work,” he said.
When asked why they chose Mannar, Subodh said: “Mannar is only an example, a metaphor. What we have done here is not just for Mannar; it is for the globe. These things are happening worldwide, not just in Mannar. The sea is rising, the heat is rising, and the people are also rising.”
The demand doesn't stop at the coast; as Bal Krishna Sah, senior correspondent at The Himalayan Times, pointed out, Nepal has been living through this.
“What Nepal has been experiencing since August 26 is evidence enough of the suffering that climate change can inflict on people who had little say in causing it, and who often do not know what is driving such a devastating disaster. If incidents like these do not make people change their ways, what will?”
Asked about the recent Nepal disaster, Subodh said investigations continue, but the people who died “had no role to play in that chunk of ice falling down.”
Climate change harms people with the least say and the least protection most, whether that’s a family in Senegal losing its home to the sea, fishermen in Mannar hauling in a tenth of their old catch, or outdoor workers in Hyderabad and Dhaka enduring dangerous heat.
An art installation by Dr Subodh Kerkar at Keeri Beach in Mannar, Sri Lanka, calls for climate justice and accountability, urging polluters to pay for the damage caused by climate change. Photo: Courtesy
Their demands are consistent: pair community observations with scientific evidence so polluters can be held accountable; fund adaptation, not just mitigation; provide shade, water, rest areas and fair pay for outdoor workers; and consult the people affected.
The speakers were careful not to overclaim. Local problems rarely have a single cause, and showing harm is not the same as proving who is to blame, so credible climate justice needs both the evidence and the accountability.
Asked what message he would leave, Subodh returned to the oldest argument.
“We have not inherited the earth from our parents or grandparents. We have borrowed it from our children. We need to give our earth back to the children in a good state. They deserve a better earth.”

item.title: More than 1,000 arrested daily as Bangladesh prisons exceed capacity
item.description:
A documentary published this week on the Facebook page of the Bangladesh Department of Prisons showcased well-furnished facilities, quality food, gymnasiums and skills development programmes for inmates. However, current and former inmates say the reality inside prisons is markedly different, as authorities struggle to manage a prison population more than double the system's capacity.
Law enforcement agencies have been arresting more than 1,000 people daily through regular and special operations aimed at curbing crime. Weapons, ammunition, drugs and locally made firearms are also being recovered during these drives.
In an operation by the Dhaka Metropolitan Police (DMP), 510 people were arrested and 48 cases filed in the capital over the past 24 hours. Despite the large number of arrests, however, crimes including murder, mugging, extortion, drug-related offences and juvenile gang activities remain difficult to control, raising concerns about the country's law and order situation.
Meanwhile, a study published in the United Kingdom has found that Bangladesh has the highest prison overcrowding rate relative to capacity among South Asian countries. For every 100 places available in the country's prisons, there are 226 inmates.
Crime analysts say arrests are only the first step towards controlling crime, arguing that proper investigations and swift justice are not being ensured. They also say criminals continue to flout the law because law enforcement agencies are failing to take sufficiently stringent measures to prevent crime.
According to DMP figures, 5,005 people were arrested on various allegations in the capital over 11 days, from October 1 to October 11. During the same period, 580 cases were filed for various offences, with the number of arrests averaging 455 a day.
Data from the Police Headquarters show that 53,518 people were arrested during special police operations between May 1 and August 26, 2026. Including approximately 150,000 arrests in other cases and operations, the total stood at 195,146, averaging around 1,650 arrests a day.
Speaking to Dhaka Tribune on Wednesday afternoon, Additional Inspector General of Police at the Police Headquarters Md Sayedur Rahman said: “Arrest is only a process of bringing a criminal under the law. Crime cannot be controlled through arrests alone. Prevention is another measure. If there is a risk of deterioration in the law and order situation somewhere, the police take preventive action.
“To reduce crime, social resistance must also be built alongside the efforts of law enforcement agencies. If someone repeatedly commits the same offence, they must be brought under exemplary punishment.”
Sri Lanka is close to Bangladesh in terms of prison overcrowding, while India and Pakistan are in comparatively better positions.
World Prison Brief (WPB), an online database maintained by the Institute for Crime and Justice Policy Research at Birkbeck, University of London, publishes statistics on prison populations worldwide. Its data on Bangladesh are based on information from the Department of Prisons.
According to WPB, Bangladesh's prisons have an official capacity of 45,186 inmates. In September this year, the prison population stood at 102,180, meaning the facilities were operating at 226.1% of their intended capacity. The country has 59 prisoners for every 100,000 people.
Data from the Department of Prisons indicate that the inmate population has increased further. As of October 14, the number of inmates stood at 130,128 against an official capacity of 45,186.
Among other South Asian countries, prison populations stand at 216% of capacity in Sri Lanka, 163% in Pakistan, 144% in Nepal, 113% in India and 112% in Myanmar.
Globally, the Republic of the Congo has the highest prison occupancy rate, at 617% of capacity. Nauru has the lowest, with its prisons holding inmates equivalent to just 14% of their intended capacity.
Speaking to Dhaka Tribune on Wednesday afternoon, Additional Inspector General of Prisons Md Jahangir Kabir said: “The 75 prisons in the country have a total capacity of 45,186 inmates. Currently, there are more than 100,000 prisoners. We struggle to manage the pressure caused by the excess number of inmates. Our workload increases, and we also have to perform additional duties.”
He added: “If a family has five members and another five guests arrive, it creates pressure on that family. We are facing the same kind of pressure.”
According to the Department of Prisons website, Bangladesh's prison system dates back to 1788, when a criminal ward was established in Dhaka. Prisons were subsequently built in Dhaka, Rajshahi, Jessore and Comilla in 1836. The Dhaka and Rajshahi prisons were declared central prisons in 1929.
The country now has 75 prisons, including 15 central prisons and 60 district prisons.
According to WPB data, 66.9% of inmates in Bangladesh's prisons are pretrial detainees. This means approximately two-thirds of those behind bars have yet to be sentenced.
Speaking to Dhaka Tribune on Wednesday evening, Assistant Inspector General of Prisons (Development) Muhammad Enayet Ullah said: “As of October 14, the total number of inmates stood at 130,128. More than 75,000 of them are awaiting trial. The number of prisoners awaiting trial is increasing the pressure on prisons.”
Although Bangladesh's prisons hold nearly three times their official capacity according to the latest Department of Prisons figures, medical services remain inadequate. Fifty-four prisons have no ambulances, while only two permanent doctors are available against 151 sanctioned positions.
The longstanding medical crisis in the country's prisons means inmates sometimes die on their way to hospitals when they require emergency treatment. Questions have also been raised about the quality of food served to prisoners, while complaints about prolonged delays in securing bail have persisted for years.
A recently released former inmate told Dhaka Tribune that overcrowding in prisons had increased significantly.
“There is no room anywhere, from the toilets to the sleeping areas. We have to live crammed together in congested conditions. It is almost as if one person's nose touches another person's nose. The food is not particularly good either. There are cockroaches, mosquitoes and flies. The excessive number of people creates a terrible stench. We have to sleep packed tightly together on the floor,” he said.
He added: “The most alarming thing is that when someone falls ill, a doctor is not available. There are also no ambulances to take them to hospital. I have seen people suffer strokes and die before my eyes, and there is nothing we can do.”
Speaking to Dhaka Tribune on Wednesday, senior Supreme Court lawyer Mohammed Saeed Ahmed Raza said: “Recently, we have seen arrests in political cases, particularly arrests followed by shown arrests. More than 1,500 people are being arrested daily. However, prisons do not have enough space to accommodate them.
“This violates the human rights of accused persons, while the excessive pressure on inmates is making the judicial system completely fragile. The state must ensure that no one remains imprisoned without committing a crime.”
According to WPB and a 2024 study, mental health conditions in prisons across Southeast Asia are a serious and neglected concern. Overcrowding and a severe shortage of mental health services have contributed to the prevalence of mental disorders among prisoners in the region, with estimates ranging from 40% to 100%.
Prison sources say each prison has a designated post for a psychiatrist, but none has a specialist in the position. Inmates in almost all prisons are living in inhumane conditions and suffering from mental and physical health problems without receiving adequate treatment.
Prisoners with health conditions require regular counselling and specialised treatment. There are also no doctors specifically assigned to care for inmates with disabilities.
Speaking to Dhaka Tribune, Additional Inspector General of Prisons Md Jahangir Kabir said: “There are no mental health specialists in prisons. If an inmate requires psychiatric treatment, we send them to the National Institute of Mental Health and Hospital. We provide medical services with assistance from district civil surgeons. We also face a shortage of ambulances.”
He said the problems had been communicated to the Ministry of Health and the relevant government departments.
Asked why crime remains difficult to control despite the large number of arrests, Dhaka University teacher and crime expert Dr Md Tawohidul Haque told Dhaka Tribune that shortcomings in law enforcement, political and social influence, and structural weaknesses were among the main reasons.
He said some accused people exploit legal loopholes and prolonged judicial proceedings to secure their release before becoming involved in crime again.
The crime expert said arrests alone could not control crime, stressing the need for impartial investigations and swift justice.

item.title: Bangladesh unaware of execution of two citizens in Saudi Arabia
item.description:
Bangladesh was unaware of the execution of two of its citizens in Makkah, Saudi Arabia, over alleged “immoral” acts at a mosque, learning of the matter only through media reports.
The Bangladesh Consulate in Jeddah subsequently wrote to the Saudi foreign ministry on Thursday, seeking details of the executions, according to sources at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in Dhaka and the consulate.
A consular source said on Friday afternoon that Saudi authorities had not formally notified Bangladesh before carrying out the executions. The consulate learned of the matter through media reports and then sought an official explanation from the Saudi foreign ministry.
The Saudi Press Agency (SPA), citing the country's Interior Ministry, confirmed the executions on Wednesday. The two Bangladeshis were identified as Nazrul Islam and Sweety Akhtar.
Middle East-based news outlet Gulf News reported that Saudi security forces had arrested the two over allegations of engaging in immoral and indecent acts at a mosque in Makkah.
According to the report, they were charged following an initial investigation and referred to court. The court sentenced them to death under ta'zir, a category of discretionary punishment under Sharia law. The judge reportedly considered the violation of the mosque's sanctity and the circumstances of the alleged offence when delivering the verdict.
Higher judicial authorities later upheld the verdict, making it final, before a royal order was issued for the executions.
In a statement, the Saudi Interior Ministry reaffirmed the government's commitment to protecting the sanctity of the holy mosques, upholding justice and enforcing Sharia law against those who violate religious sanctity. It also warned that similar offences at holy sites would attract severe punishment.
Private sources in Saudi Arabia said the trial had been underway at a court in Jeddah for several months. Two prominent Bangladeshi citizens reportedly assisted in the proceedings as interpreters.
Bangladesh and Saudi Arabia are both parties to the Vienna Convention on Consular Relations. Under Article 36, if a foreign national is arrested, the detaining country must inform the person's consulate without delay if the detainee requests it and facilitate consular communication and assistance.
It remains unclear whether the two Bangladeshis had requested that the Bangladeshi consulate be notified.
Several officials at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the executions were unlikely to have taken place immediately after the arrests, given the judicial process involved. They also questioned why no one acting on behalf of the two had contacted the Bangladeshi mission during their detention.
No information has yet emerged about the nature or duration of the two Bangladeshis' stay in Saudi Arabia, or whether they received legal assistance or had an opportunity to appeal during the proceedings.

item.title: Shyamsiddhir Math - a monument that pierces the sky
item.description:
A couple of weeks ago, on a crisp morning, I found myself cruising down the beautiful Dhaka-Mawa Highway. I was heading towards Sreenagar in Munshiganj. All along the route, the fluffy white feathers of catkin bushes danced between the asphalt and the parallel rail tracks—a breathtaking visual testimony to the arrival of autumn.
While my final destination for the day was Arial Beel, a vast wetland, I decided to take a spontaneous detour at Shyamsiddhi, a Union under Sreenagar. There lays a hidden gem, tucked away in the tranquility of rural life – Shyamsiddhir Math. This math is a two-century-old architectural marvel that pierces the sky.
A closer view of the Shyamsiddhir Math, looking upward through the surrounding lush greenery and coconut palm fronds. Dhaka Tribune/Collected
I am no stranger to math monuments in Bangladesh, having explored many across different regions, including the famous Sonarang Twin Math in the neighboring Tongibari Upazila. Yet, nothing quite prepares you for the sheer scale of Shyamsiddhir Math. Standing at an imposing height estimated anything between 220 to 240 feet, it easily dwarfs the others.
The structure features complex brick ornamentation at its octagonal base and transitions into a sharply tapered conical spire. Though weathered over time, it remains an architectural marvel and a significant tourist attraction in the Munshiganj region. Dhaka Tribune/Collected
Built in the early 19th century by a wealthy merchant named Shambunath Majumdar to honor his deceased father, historical records note it as the tallest math in Bangladesh and one of the highest in the entire Indian subcontinent. The slight variation in its exact recorded height depends on whether you include the ancient, massive iron trident that still proudly crowns the apex of its spire.
For travel writers, spelling math in English is always a bit of a riddle, given its myriad South Asian variants like matha, moth, or mutt. Linguistic nuances aside, the very concept of math carries diverse connotations. While its Sanskrit root refers to a monastery or a place of learning for monks, the word has evolved in our part of the world. Today, it can mean a Hindu monastery, an ashram, or—most commonly—a distinctive, cone-shaped commemorative monument.
The lower left corner features a modern white sign written in Bengali script. It reads: Shri Shri Sarbojonin Shiba Math, Shyamsiddhi, Location: Adjacent to Shyamsiddhi Union Parishad, Srinagar, Munshiganj, Built in 1836. Dhaka Tribune/Collected
My own travels confirm that across rural Bangladesh and near old Zamindari (landlord) estates, these tall, slender, sharply pointed structures function primarily as cremation monuments (Chita Mandir). Built over the cremation sites of prominent landlords, saints, or family elders, they serve as soaring, brick-and-mortar tributes to the deceased.
The renovated ground-level entrance door facade to the main inner sanctum at the base of the math. Over the years, the lower base section was modernized with these white tiles and printed pictures of Lord Shiva, complete with the prominent red arch trim over the main entrance. Dhaka Tribune/Collected
Approaching the site through a neighborhood dotted with traditional tin and wooden stilt houses, the dense greenery surrounding the monument caught my eye first. Then there was that unforgettable sight and sound of pandemonium of parakeets hovering overhead before diving back into the structure.
Over the years, structural decay has created hundreds of tiny crevices and holes near the top tier. Nature has beautifully reclaimed this decay, organically transforming the ancient monument into a lively bird sanctuary. Framed by thriving coconut, mango, and guava trees, the upper sections of the tapered monument also host opportunistic parasitic vegetation. Small wild fig and banyan saplings stubbornly take root directly out of the high brick fissures.
The hollow alcoves within the tower make it a famous sanctuary for hundreds of parakeets. Dhaka Tribune/Collected
Architecturally, Shyamsiddhir Math is a masterclass in 19th-century artisanship. It is a robust, octagonal brick structure built using traditional chun-surki — a highly durable heritage mortar made of slaked lime and powdered burnt clay. Its structural blueprint features a base measuring 21 feet in both length and width (though some archaeological records classify the external bounding box as a six-meter square) with foundational walls stretching roughly a meter deep.
These numerous deep square recesses scattered across the octagonal brick walls are the exact openings where hundreds of wild parakeets and parrots build their nests, making the structure a prominent local ecological attraction. Dhaka Tribune/Collected
The monument rises in three distinct vertical stages: at the base – a lower square section serving as the primary sanctum, featuring a prominent entrance adorned with a pointed arch on its southern façade; in mid-section – heavy brickwork begins to taper inward; and finally an internal chamber that seamlessly transitions into a narrowing spire stretches up to its pinnacle.
The writer standing in front of a beautifully crafted, elevated wooden house just opposite to the Shyamsiddhir Math. Built in a traditional regional architectural style, this house features white wall panels, dark wood frames, and ornate geometric latticework along the roofline. Dhaka Tribune/Collected
Today, these heavily perforated upper exterior walls are a thriving ecological haven. Inhabited by hundreds of native birds—predominantly parakeets and crested mynas—the ancient brickwork stays vibrantly alive with their chirping.
This mid-angle perspective captures the sweeping, upward taper of the Shyamsiddhir Math, emphasizing its immense scale against the rural skyline. If one looks closely at the upper edges and crevices, s/he can see small dark silhouettes of birds perched along the sides, highlighting its lively status as a natural aviary. Dhaka Tribune/ Collected
Long after I left the premises and advanced toward the sweeping waters of Arial Beel, I could still see the math's spire slicing through the horizon from miles away. It stands like a historic lighthouse over the green plains of Munshiganj—a poetic reminder of past craftsmanship, familial love, and the wild resilience of nature.
