item.title: Five killed in fire at Cox’s Bazar resort
item.description:
At least five people have died in a fire at Tup-Tup Resort in the Patuartek area near Inani Beach in Ukhia upazila of Cox’s Bazar.
The fire broke out around 7am on Saturday at the resort along Marine Drive. Fire Service officials and police have warned that the death toll could rise.
Senior Fire Service official Dolan Acharya confirmed that five bodies had been recovered. The victims are believed to be tourists, but their identities could not be immediately established.
Ukhia police station Officer-in-Charge Atiqur Rahman said the death toll might increase as rescue workers continued searching the site. Police are working to establish the victims’ identities and determine the total number of casualties.
According to the fire service, three firefighting units reached the scene around 8am and began operations. The blaze was brought under control around 10am, after which rescuers began searching the resort.
The resort, built primarily of wood, sustained extensive damage. Firefighters are continuing to search the building for anyone who may remain trapped inside.
Local residents said the resort’s staff and management left the scene after the fire broke out.
The cause of the fire, the extent of the damage and whether the resort had adequate fire safety measures remain unclear.

item.title: A card is not a safety net if the poor remain invisible
item.description:
A garment worker loses her job. A riverbank family is displaced. A widow suddenly becomes the sole provider for her children. Their circumstances can change overnight; a government beneficiary list may not.
That time lag is not just a clerical inconvenience. For a household already choosing between food and medicine, a temporary hardship can turn into lasting poverty.
This is why Bangladesh's latest social protection exercise deserves more scrutiny than the excitement surrounding a new card.
On October 12, the government began nationwide door-to-door collection of household information for the Family Card program. Officials say the database is intended to cover approximately 45 million households, with data collection due to conclude on November 30.
It is an ambitious administrative undertaking. But its success will depend less on the number of entries gathered than on the number of vulnerable families no longer falling through the cracks.
The World Bank's October 2026 Bangladesh Development update offers a sobering benchmark. It estimates that the number of people living in poverty increased by approximately 2.1 million in FY2025-26, while about half of the poorest households remain outside social protection programs.
These findings should be read together. At precisely the moment when more families need a cushion, the existing system struggles to reach many who are already at the bottom.
For too long, our public conversation has treated social protection as a contest of allocations: How many schemes, how many beneficiaries, how many billions of taka. Those figures matter, but they cannot establish whether assistance is timely, adequate, or fairly targeted.
A benefit announced is not necessarily a benefit received; a name on a list is not an assurance of future eligibility; and a card in a wallet does not, by itself, protect a family against the next shock.
The central policy challenge is what economists call exclusion error: Households that qualify for assistance are left out.
At the same time, inclusion errors can direct scarce resources to those who do not qualify. Perfect targeting is impossible, but both forms of error can be measured and reduced.
The new exercise relies on a proxy means test to estimate household welfare from observable characteristics. That is more systematic than selection by discretion alone, yet a score cannot fully capture a sudden dismissal, an expensive illness, or the loss of land to a river. A statistical estimate should guide an eligibility decision, not make it immune to challenge.
An announced benefit is not necessarily a benefit received; a card in a wallet is not protection against the next shock.
The government's stated plan to receive appeals online and through union parishad service centres is therefore important. But an appeal mechanism is meaningful only if it works for people with limited literacy, poor connectivity, or no local influence.
Applicants should receive intelligible reasons for rejection, a tracking number, and a decision within a published period. Independent spot checks and public reporting on overturned decisions could separate a functioning grievance system from a mere box for collecting complaints.
Even a carefully constructed database can become obsolete. A household above the eligibility threshold today may fall below it after an illness, a price shock, or river erosion.
Bangladesh needs its planned dynamic social registry to work as a continuously updated public service, rather than a one-off enumeration exercise.
Households must be able to report changes without incurring expensive travel or relying on unofficial intermediaries. In disaster-affected localities, rapid reassessments should be possible without waiting for another nationwide survey.
This matters particularly in the informal economy, where fluctuating earnings rarely appear in conventional employment records.
Program design poses a second challenge. Issuing the Family Card in a woman's name is a potentially valuable recognition of her economic agency. Yet, deprivation is not identical for every member of a household.
An older person requiring care, a person with a disability, and a child facing malnutrition need different combinations of services. Integrating databases and eliminating unnecessary duplication are sensible objectives.
Replacing every specialized program with an undifferentiated household payment would not be sensible. The goal should be a common gateway to appropriately tailored support.
Privacy must be treated as a condition of inclusion, not an afterthought. A registry on this scale will contain sensitive information about identities, assets, and family circumstances. Without safeguards, it could expose vulnerable people to data misuse or unjust exclusion.
Information collection should be proportionate to need, access restricted to official roles, changes auditable, and errors correctable by the households concerned. Program performance should be transparent; recipients' private circumstances should not be.
There will be a familiar objection: Bangladesh cannot afford administrative perfection while its budget is under strain. The fiscal constraint is real.
According to the World Bank, revenue collection stood at only 8.3% of GDP in FY2025-26, and economic growth is projected at 3.4% in FY2026-27. Yet scarcity strengthens the case for accuracy.
Every avoidable duplicate payment, unresolved exclusion, or delayed transfer carries a higher social cost when the fiscal room for correction is so narrow. Better targeting is not a substitute for adequate funding; it is a way to improve the impact of that funding.
Indeed, the World Bank estimates that, under a reform scenario combining better-targeted existing cash programs, food-subsidy consolidation, and the Family Card, an additional 2.85 million people could be lifted out of poverty, and this is a modelled possibility, not an assured outcome.
It nevertheless illustrates why the quality of implementation matters. Nor should the reform agenda be reduced to austerity. Removing subsidies before dependable compensation reaches vulnerable households would shift the burden of adjustment onto those least able to bear it.
A credible reform program should publish a modest set of results every quarter: The share of the poorest households receiving assistance, the time between approval and first payment, the proportion of grievances resolved, payment failure rates, and whether women can access transfers without intermediaries.
District-level comparisons, with appropriate privacy safeguards, would help locate persistent gaps. An independent evaluation after the first year would reveal far more than a ceremony celebrating cards distributed.
Ultimately, social protection is about the relationship between citizens and the state. A fair system does not require a family to prove its desperation repeatedly or to rely on familiarity with an official. It recognizes vulnerability, responds when circumstances change, and explains decisions that affect people's lives.
Bangladesh has an opportunity to make the Family Card more than another symbol of welfare reform. The next milestone should not simply be the completion of a national database. It should be the moment when an eligible household can trust that need, rather than connections or procedural luck, determines access to assistance.
A safety net earns its name not when a card is issued, but when someone falling is actually caught.
Dr Munshi Muhammad Abdul Kader Jilani holds a PhD in Knowledge Management from Wuhan University of Technology in China. He is currently working as an Assistant Professor at the Bangladesh Institute of Governance and Management (BIGM), University of Dhaka (Affiliated), and Associate Editor of the BIGM Journal of Policy Analysis.

item.title: Memory as identity, memory as a file cabinet
item.description:
Recently, we lost a dear family friend who lived to the remarkable age of 100 years and 9 months. She attended our wedding back in the late 1970s, and we remained in touch over the years.
During the last two decades especially, we visited her frequently in Paris. Now that she is gone, our memories of her live on, providing us with a source of comfort and contentment, and serving as a kind of shock absorber as we come to terms with her loss.
She lived in Bangladesh as a UN official, and had contributed to the women’s developmental issues in the mid-1970s. Bangladesh had a special place in her heart. She would always read my pieces -- even after she turned 100 -- and share her comments when we called her for long chats. I always found her feedback thoughtful and uplifting.
She would also advise me to read something she discovered. Decades ago, she introduced me to the works of philosopher Rene Girard (1923-2015) -- almost her namesake; ours was Renee Gerard (1926-2026).
Remembering her company, advice, chats in her book-filled living room in Paris, or having a meal at a Parisian restaurant gave me the idea of writing on memories. Suddenly, I remembered what our English teacher KPC (Kali Prashad Chaterjee) at Bagerhat High School taught us when elucidating William Wordsworth’s poem The Daffodils. KPC, summarizing the poem, told us that you find joy twice: First, by seeing the daffodils in the lake, and then again by remembering them.
This is what human memory does. It is not an archive we consult but a place we return to -- and we come back changed, often with a smile on our face.
Imagine life without memory. Each moment would arrive without a past and depart without a future to hold it. We could still eat, work, and move through the day, but nothing would add up.
A life lived only in the now is a series of disjointed events, not a story. It is memory that turns events into a biography, and a biography into an identity. We know who we are because we remember who we have been, and whom we have been with.
Nowhere is this clearer than in grief. When someone we love dies, what remains is not a file but a relationship that continues inside us. I remember my mother's laughter while reading Shibram Chakraborty, or Syed Mujtaba Ali. I remember a teacher's scolding, or a rare, hard-won praise.
These memories hurt, yet they also hold us. They remind us that we were loved, that we belonged somewhere, that someone's life was woven into ours.
Mourning is, in large part, the slow work of converting an absence into a memory we can live with. The dead do not leave us entirely so long as we remember them, and in remembering them we remember ourselves.
Memory also gives us a sense of direction. We recall the choices that led us here, the sacrifices others made, the values we were handed and the ones we chose. From these we draw purpose. A person who remembers a parent's quiet persistence may find the strength to persist. A person who remembers a friend's generosity may decide to be generous.
Human memory is also practical. We use it to solve problems, to recall what Marx said and where -- “peasants are like potatoes in a sack” in the Eighteenth Brumaire -- as students remain impressed. Memory helps us learn, plan, and function. In this respect, it resembles the memory of a computer, which also stores information and retrieves it when needed.
The comparison is tempting, and it is useful as far as it goes. Both kinds of memory help a system get things done.
But the parallel ends there. A computer's memory is functional through and through. It stores data in order to process it, and it retrieves data in order to complete a task. When a hard drive holds 10,000 photographs, none of them is more precious than another unless a program is told to rank them. Nothing in the machine aches when a file is deleted. Nothing is consoled when a file is restored. The memory serves the operation and has no stake in what it holds.
The newest AI systems, for all their astonishing fluency, do not change this. They can recall vast amounts of information, summarize a life, even write a convincing elegy. They can store and retrieve what we tell them about our parents.
Yet storing is not remembering.
There is, as far as we can tell, no one inside who is comforted by the retrieval, no one for whom the stored detail is a loss or a gift. These systems generate words about meaning without, so far as we know, experiencing meaning.
Their memory is a tool. Ours is a part of who we are.
There is a quiet lesson here about how we live: If memory is where meaning is made, then we have a responsibility to tend to it. We can ask our elders for their stories before it is too late. We can name the people who shaped us and tell their stories to the young. We can resist the thin, hurried present in which nothing is remembered because nothing is allowed to matter.
A culture that stops remembering together -- in rituals, anniversaries, and family tables -- will find that it has plenty of data and very little meaning.
At its core, computer memory is a vast digital filing system built on billions of microscopic electronic switches called transistors, but it has no emotion, least consciousness. Its functional power lies in speed and exact replication: It can store billions of these tiny data points, execute complex calculations, and retrieve files with absolute precision in nanoseconds without ever degrading, misremembering, or imbuing a single byte with emotion.
Computers will keep getting better at storing everything. What they cannot do, at least for now, is care about what they store.
That is our work, and also our gift. We remember -- not only to function, but to belong, to grieve, to love, and to go on.
Habibul Haque Khondker is a sociologist and columnist.

item.title: Doing all we can to reduce poverty
item.description:
As the world observed the International Day for Eradication of Poverty, it is clear that our national reflections must be anchored in sobering reality rather than complacent rhetoric.
The World Bank’s latest revelations -- confirming that our GDP growth has slumped to a dismal 3.4% and that over 2 million additional people have been pushed into poverty over the past year -- expose what must be identified as a profound socio-economic crisis.
For a nation that long aspired towards double digit growth, to have been reduced to below 4% for consecutive years is a significant blow. We must also contend with the fact that nearly 62 million citizens live just above the poverty line, meaning a single health shock, price spike, or market disruption can plunge entire families back into extreme hardship.
To that end, poverty eradication remains a distant dream for our country, and that is the reality. However, addressing it, and ensuring that we pull people out of poverty every day instead, is an urgent national emergency.
For too long, our poverty alleviation strategies have relied on fragmented, leaky safety programs that frequently miss the poorest segments of society while misallocating resources. While we are looking to change that narrative with the Family Card program, we must ensure that we get this right.
It goes without saying that a nation striving for structural reform can no longer tolerate a system where wealth inequality widens while the vulnerable absorb the harshest blows of economic stagnation.
Reducing poverty must go beyond merely managing destitution for our population. While the short term requires us to pull more and more people out of extreme poverty, the end goal must be to fix our macroeconomic foundations, drive job creation, and ensure that economic recovery lifts every citizen, not just a privileged few.
The end goal must always be to become an equitable nation, not merely a prosperous one.

item.title: Dhaka's air quality remains 'unhealthy'
item.description:
The air quality in Dhaka remained unhealthy on Saturday morning, with an Air Quality Index (AQI) score of 166 at 9:14am.
With this score, the capital ranked ninth among the world's most polluted cities.
Iraq’s Baghdad, Singapore’s Singapore, Pakistan’s Lahore and India’s Mumbai occupied the top four spots on the list, with AQI scores of 378, 206, 201 and 192, respectively.
An AQI score between 50 and 100 is considered "moderate" with an acceptable air quality, while one between 101 and 150 is considered "unhealthy for sensitive groups", while a score between 151 and 200 is classified as "unhealthy."
AQI readings between 201 and 300 are termed "very unhealthy", and anything above 301 is considered "hazardous", posing serious health risks.
The AQI provides daily updates on air quality, indicating how clean or polluted the air is and highlighting potential health impacts.
In Bangladesh, the AQI is calculated based on five major pollutants: particulate matter (PM10 and PM2.5), nitrogen dioxide (NO2), carbon monoxide (CO), sulfur dioxide (SO2) and ozone.
Dhaka has long struggled with air pollution, with air quality typically deteriorating during winter and improving during the monsoon season.
The World Health Organization estimates that air pollution causes around seven million deaths globally each year, mainly from stroke, heart disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, lung cancer and acute respiratory infections.

item.title: Former additional secretary found dead at Officers Club
item.description:
The body of former additional secretary Md Mosharraf Hossain was recovered from a building under construction at the Officers Club in Dhaka’s Ramna area on Friday morning.
Police recovered the body around 11:45am.
Mosharraf Hossain, a member of the Officers Club, lived with his family in Banani.
According to reports, he arrived at the club around 10am with his youngest daughter. He left her near the swimming pool, beside the building under construction, and entered the structure.
About an hour later, his body was found in a bloodied condition on the ground floor near a staircase.
Sheikh Zahidul Islam, deputy commissioner of the Dhaka Metropolitan Police’s Ramna division, said Mosharraf had poor eyesight and apparently fell from the third floor into an open space on the ground floor.
“We have completed the preliminary examination of the body,” he said.
The deputy commissioner said the family had requested that no post-mortem examination be conducted and that the body would be handed over to them.
Mosharraf’s eldest daughter lives in the United States. According to the family, his burial will take place after she arrives in Bangladesh.

item.title: Man Utd have 'moved on' from Martinez outburst, says Carrick
item.description:
Michael Carrick said Friday that Manchester United had "moved on" from Lisandro Martinez's outburst aimed at the club's hierarchy, stressing it was "really not a drama for us as a group".
Argentina defender Martinez took aim at the United hierarchy following their 2-0 Champions League loss to Atletico Madrid on Tuesday, saying Carrick had been left with an under-strength squad.
The centre-back criticised technical director Jason Wilcox, saying he had "100 percent" expected more investment during the summer transfer window after United finished third in the Premier League last season.
It is understood Martinez, who issued an apology on Thursday, has been fined for his outburst.
United manager Carrick confirmed during a pre-match press conference on Friday that Martinez would be in his squad for their Premier League match at bitter rivals Leeds on Sunday.
Carrick, under intense pressure after a terrible start to the season, was asked by reporters about Martinez's comments and subsequent developments.
"We've moved on from that, it was one of those things," he said. "I think Licha (Martinez) has come out and acknowledged the situation and as a group we've moved on.
"It's really not a drama for us as a group, I think the boys have trained really well. This morning there was a really good feeling around the squad."
Martinez, 28, said in a statement he had held positive talks with the club's leadership and Carrick.
"Everyone knows that I am a passionate person and that I live football with great intensity," he said in a post on Instagram.
"The frustration of the defeat led me to express how I felt at a time and place that perhaps were not the right ones, and for that I want to apologise."
- 'Emotion' -
Former United captain Roy Keane has branded the situation at his former club "a bit of a circus".
Carrick was pressed by reporters on the nature of the apology from Martinez, which did not mention Wilcox by name.
"I think he (Martinez) has released his statement and he's realised he's made a mistake," said the United boss. "I think that's enough for all of us to move on with."
He added: "I understand the emotion at times. We ask for passion, we ask for emotion, we ask for fire and we ask for players to care.
"There's a way of doing that and that's already been acknowledged. We need to carry that. We need to carry that intensity and that willingness and that togetherness and that spirit and everything."
United have made their worst start to a league season in 40 years.
They are 13th in the Premier League, with just one win from six matches, but Carrick, a former United and England midfielder, deflected a question about the pressure on him personally.
"I don't need results, we all need results," he said. "It's not about me. Manchester United is a lot bigger than any individual, bigger than me.
"Bigger than any player, anyone else who works at this football club. It always has been, and it's not about me."

item.title: Mohammedan, Kings clinch BFL victories
item.description:
Mohammedan Sporting Club continued their winning run in the Bangladesh Football League with a 2–0 victory over PWD Sports Club, while Bashundhara Kings registered a comfortable 3–0 win over City Club on Friday.
At Shaheed Miraj-Tapan Stadium in Manikganj, Mohammedan secured their third consecutive victory thanks to goals from Malian forward Souleymane Diabate and midfielder Minhazul Abedin Rakib.
Diabate broke the deadlock soon after the break, scoring in the 47th minute to put the traditional Motijheel outfit ahead.
Rakib then sealed the victory with the second goal in the 78th minute, ensuring Mohammedan collected all three points.
PWD attempted to fight back but failed to find the net as Mohammedan maintained their winning momentum.
The victory took Mohammedan to nine points from three matches, while PWD remained on three points after four outings.
Meanwhile, Bashundhara Kings returned to winning ways with a 3–0 victory over City Club at Shaheed Barkat Stadium in Gazipur.
Brazilian forward Robson Azevedo da Silva took the lead in the 49th minute. Nigerian forward Chukwuiebube Emeka Ogbugh doubled the lead from the penalty spot in the 72nd minute.
Midfielder Sayed Shah Quazem Kirmanee completed the rout with a third goal four minutes into the stoppage time.
The victory was Kings’ second in the league, taking their tally to seven points from three matches. City Club also have seven points but have played four matches.
In Saturday’s fourth-round fixtures, Abahani Limited, Dhaka, will take on Chattogram City Football Club at Mymensingh District Stadium.
Rahmatganj Muslim Friends Society will face Brothers Union at Birshreshtha Flight Lieutenant Matiur Rahman Stadium in Munshiganj, while Bangladesh Police Football Club will meet Arambagh Krira Sangha at Shaheed Barkat Stadium in Gazipur.

item.title: Ending the culture of violence against journalists
item.description:
The killing of a journalist in Netrokona is another grim reminder of the dangers faced by those who investigate wrongdoing and bring uncomfortable truths to public attention.
Such attacks carry consequences that extend far beyond the individual victim: They threaten the public’s right to information and undermine the very foundations of accountability.
Lutfuzzaman Alif Fakir, a Netrokona correspondent for Ruposhi Bangla who frequently reported on corruption through his page Detective Article, was shot dead by unidentified assailants in Durgapur on Thursday night. He had previously survived a violent attack in November of last year.
This tragedy raises serious questions about whether adequate protective measures were taken following that prior incident.
It must be made clear: This culture of violence against journalists is completely unacceptable and must be brought under control.
The authorities must treat this killing with the urgency it demands. The perpetrators must be identified, arrested, and brought to justice through a prompt and transparent investigation.
Without accountability, those who resort to violence to silence the press will only feel emboldened.
However, seeking justice after a killing is not enough. Bangladesh urgently needs a proactive system to safeguard journalists before threats escalate into tragedy.
Complaints of intimidation and physical violence must be investigated immediately, backed by credible risk assessments and timely protection. Local law enforcement must take threats against reporters seriously -- especially when victims have already experienced violence.
Media organizations also share a duty to establish safety protocols, provide legal assistance, and stand by journalists facing danger due to their work. Freelancers and local correspondents, who often operate with limited institutional support, must not be left behind.
A free press cannot function when journalists are forced to choose between speaking the truth and preserving their lives. Nor can citizens expect corruption and abuse of power to be exposed if those who investigate them are left exposed to harm.
This tragedy must spur concrete action. Protecting journalists is nothing less than protecting democracy itself.

item.title: Strikes hit airport complex in Yemen's govt-held Aden, Houthis claim attack
item.description:
Two missiles landed Friday within the perimeter of the airport in the Yemeni city of Aden, the interim capital of the Saudi-backed government, authorities said, with the Houthis claiming the attack.
The Houthis are fighting both Yemen's internationally recognised government and their Saudi allies.
In a statement attributed to a military source, the Houthis said an attack targeted "the Saudi forces' command headquarters in the Badr camp in Aden province" as well as a weapons depot.
An AFP journalist heard two loud explosions from the vicinity of the airport, but was not in a position to confirm what precisely had been hit.
The Yemeni information ministry said in a statement that a Yemenia Airways flight from Aden to Cairo narrowly missed being struck.
It was "preparing for takeoff at the very moment when the terrorist Houthi militia targeted the airport with two missiles that landed approximately 500 metres from the aircraft and about 100 metres from the centre of the runway," a statement said.
"What occurred was not merely an assault on a civilian airport, but a direct threat to the lives of passengers and flight crews, to aviation safety, and a grave violation of international laws and norms."
The Aden Capital Security Department said in a statement "that two rockets launched by the Houthi movement landed inside the Aden International Airport complex, in the second incident of its kind in less than a week".
"According to preliminary information, no loss of life was recorded as a result of the incident."
